solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: (& 17dn.) Balls harmed by this typical tabloid-like response to events?

blocks.note: surface reading: something that injures a man's testicles, a blow below the belt
setter's reading: the instant, unthinking outrage a tabloid headline produces; the blow to the balls comes from the joint in the leg

explanation.surface: A crude joke about a groin injury doubling as a jab at reflexive tabloid outrage.
explanation.walkthrough: The first phrase hints at a knee in the groin; the whole names the reflex response tabloids are known for. Two halves of one phrase share the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes an automatic, unconsidered reply, like the reflex a doctor tests by tapping below the kneecap.

clue.text: see 11ac.
Hitler lover and Nigel Farage's extreme elements rise, taking Conservative line: "Country besieged by foreigners!"

indicators.note: the extreme elements of a phrase are its outermost letters, the very first and very last
a word taking others in holds them inside itself
in a down entry, rising means the letters are read from bottom to top

blocks.note: Eva Braun was Hitler's companion
L is the abbreviation for line
C is the abbreviation for Conservative
the first letter of Nigel and the last of Farage

explanation.surface: A dig at far-right rhetoric, pairing Hitler with Farage and a xenophobic slogan about a country overrun by foreigners.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted slogan sounds like a far-right complaint, but read literally it is a dictionary definition. Hitler's lover is Eva Braun.
explanation.definitionFit: An enclave is a territory wholly surrounded by another state's land, so it is ringed on every side by foreign ground.

clue.text: Slight perpetrated by tabloid in column

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: a file is a column of people, one behind another
a rag is a disparaging word for a low-quality newspaper

explanation.surface: A tabloid columnist delivers an insult in print.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slight' reads as a noun, an insult, but it is the adjective meaning frail; a file is a line of soldiers one behind another.
explanation.definitionFit: Something slight is delicate or flimsy, easily broken, which is exactly what fragile describes.

clue.text: One with brass (and more) gets daughter and mothers framed in jest

indicators.note: something framed in another is surrounded by it on all sides

blocks.note: banter is joking talk
D is the abbreviation for daughter
ma is an informal word for mother; two of them are mas

explanation.surface: Someone with brass neck winds up being teased about his daughter and mothers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brass' suggests cheek or money, but means the brass instruments of a band; the bracket admits a band may have other instruments too.
explanation.definitionFit: A bandmaster conducts a band, typically a brass band, which may include other instruments too, hence the bracketed extra.

clue.text: Rustic dancing, it might well bring tears to your eyes

definitions.text: it might well bring tears to your eyes

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and end up in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A country dance so awful it is enough to make you weep.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sounds like an emotional reaction to the dancing, but it is literal: a squirt of juice stings the eyes.
explanation.definitionFit: Juice from lemons, limes and oranges is acidic, and a spray of it in the face makes eyes sting and water.

clue.text: 'Unique' alternative Con. candidate's termination – never again!

indicators.note: an alternative version of a word is an altered arrangement of its letters
a word's termination is where it ends, its final letter

blocks.note: the only one of its kind is unique
taken as written, then rearranged
the final letter of candidate

explanation.surface: A Conservative candidate's career ends, and voters vow never to repeat the mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something on a single occasion only means it will not be repeated in future.

clue.text: Love to pursue heavy breathing sort of entertainment!

indicators.note: one thing pursuing another comes behind it, so it is placed after

blocks.note: to pant is to breathe heavily
love is zero in tennis, and zero looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A lover chasing someone while panting, hinting at a seedy sort of show.
explanation.walkthrough: A panto (pantomime) is a British Christmas stage show for families, full of slapstick and audience shouting.
explanation.definitionFit: Pantomime is a traditional British genre of family stage show, a particular kind of theatrical amusement.

clue.text: (& 24ac.) CIA/Bush rip-off, the making of Bush

indicators.note: off means gone wrong, so the letters are disordered

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dig at the CIA and President Bush plagiarising something, the making of his presidency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bush' reads as the US president, but in the definition it is slang for a woman's pubic hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Bush is slang for the hair in the groin, and the individual strands make it up.

clue.text: Account of events – managed to spin a fair share?

indicators.note: to spin something round turns it to face the opposite way

blocks.note: to run a business is to manage it
a ration is an allotted portion

explanation.surface: Someone manages to spin the story so they get their fair share, a political-press picture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spin' suggests media spin on an account of events, which suits the surface, but its job is purely to turn a word round.
explanation.definitionFit: A narration is the telling of a story, a spoken or written report of what happened.

clue.text: "Bust top class!" – member's attempt at verbal encouragement

blocks.note: to bust something is to break it
A is the top grade or class
a leg is a limb, or member, of the body

explanation.surface: An exclamation urging someone to smash the upper class.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is a theatrical good-luck wish, said instead of 'good luck', which actors consider unlucky.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre people wish performers success with this idiom, a superstitious way of cheering them on before a show.

clue.text: (& 2dn.) Unpleasant duty of sullied Labour

blocks.note: something sullied is soiled
labour is toil

explanation.surface: A jibe at the tarnished Labour Party and its distasteful obligations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' looks like the political party; here it simply means toil.
explanation.definitionFit: Dirty work is a disagreeable or dishonest task, often one nobody else wants to take on.

clue.text: Put a tick against broadcast moody writer

indicators.note: a broadcast is heard rather than seen, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: to check off an item on a list is to mark it with a tick

explanation.surface: A reviewer marks down a gloomy author on air.
explanation.walkthrough: Anton Chekhov was the Russian playwright and short-story writer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian dramatist's plays are famously melancholy and brooding, full of wistful, gloomy characters.

clue.text: Balls squeezed by tight chinos – it's voluptuous?

indicators.note: tight means drunk, and drunken letters stagger into a new order
something squeezed by another is pressed inside it

blocks.note: Ed Balls is a former Labour politician
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man's crotch squeezed by too-tight trousers, a sight of questionable sensuality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' suggests anatomy, but it is the Labour politician Ed Balls; 'tight' is British slang for drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: A hedonist pursues pleasure, and a voluptuous life is one devoted to sensual luxury and gratification.

clue.text: Covert affair in Australia is one-sided

indicators.note: the letters sought lie within the run of words that follows

blocks.note: the letters span the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A secret fling conducted down under that is all on one side.
explanation.definitionFit: A liaison is a secret sexual relationship, typically an illicit one conducted behind a partner's back.

clue.text: see 26dn.
Resting-place in which Clinton grabs too blasted hard?

indicators.note: blasted things are blown apart and scattered
something that grabs others holds them within its grip

blocks.note: Bill Clinton, the former US president
taken as written, then rearranged
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Bill Clinton grabbing someone too roughly, with a nod to his scandals.
explanation.walkthrough: Boot Hill is the traditional name for a Wild West cemetery where gunfighters were buried with their boots on.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a frontier graveyard, and a grave is a final place of repose for the dead.

clue.text: His employer's taken in by the hard going Blunt

indicators.note: the named letter is going, so it is dropped from the word
something taken in by another is received inside it

blocks.note: taken as written, then shortened
H is the abbreviation for hard
ER (Elizabeth Regina) employs His Majesty's servants; ER's gives ERS

explanation.surface: A servant's employer being taken in, things getting tough, and someone named Blunt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blunt' with its capital looks like a name, perhaps the royal art adviser Anthony Blunt, but it means curt.
explanation.definitionFit: A terse remark is brief to the point of rudeness, as is a blunt one.

clue.text: see 1dn.
Adroit appropriation of old British company, which falls short of what's required

definitions.text: which falls short of what's required

indicators.note: appropriating something means taking it into your own possession, so it ends up held inside

blocks.note: deft means skilful
ICI, Imperial Chemical Industries, was a major British firm

explanation.surface: A clever takeover of a former British firm that leaves the books in the red.
explanation.walkthrough: ICI was Imperial Chemical Industries, a giant of British industry broken up in the 2000s, hence 'old'.
explanation.definitionFit: A deficit is a shortfall, the amount by which money or resources fall below what is needed.

clue.text: Old movie star, mainly pissed, acquiring Oscar finally

indicators.note: pissed is British slang for drunk, and drunken letters reel into a new order
finally points to the last letter of the word before

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letter of Oscar

explanation.surface: A faded film star, mostly drunk, finally picks up an Oscar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mainly' looks like it means 'mostly', but it is the letters to be rearranged. Oscar is also the radio code word for O, a false trail here.
explanation.definitionFit: Marilyn Monroe was a Hollywood screen icon of the 1950s, known widely by her first name alone.

clue.text: Unsavoury sort of topless scene often taken by PC types

indicators.note: without its top, a word loses its first letter
to sort something is to rearrange it into a different order

blocks.note: food that is off has gone bad
taken as written, then cut and rearranged

explanation.surface: A sleazy topless scene that politically correct people are bound to object to.
explanation.walkthrough: PC means politically correct; the definition plays on the idiom 'to take offence'.
explanation.definitionFit: People who are quick to feel insulted are said to take umbrage, and the noun completes that common idiom.

clue.text: Manservant causes row about dead royal 'rising up'

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising up means the letters are read from the bottom
about means around, so one word wraps the other

blocks.note: a fray is a fight or quarrel
Princess Diana, known as Di, who died in 1997

explanation.surface: A servant stirs up a row about a dead royal coming back to life.
explanation.walkthrough: Man Friday is the servant in Robinson Crusoe, and the name became a term for a loyal assistant.
explanation.definitionFit: In Defoe's novel Robinson Crusoe's loyal helper is named after the weekday, and the name came to mean any faithful aide.

clue.text: Broadcast on Boris's centre support: it's a bomb-dropping event

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letter

blocks.note: to air a programme is to broadcast it
the middle letter of Boris
aid is help

explanation.surface: A broadcast backing Boris Johnson turns out to be a bombshell.
explanation.definitionFit: During a raid from the sky, aircraft attack a target by releasing explosives over it.

clue.text: Miliband's tip: "Woes out of hand? Make use of a pointer"

indicators.note: the tip is the end of a word, here its final letter
things out of hand are out of control, so the letters run wild

blocks.note: the final letter of Miliband
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Ed Miliband's advice for troubles spiralling: get someone to point the way.
explanation.walkthrough: The pointer is a dowsing rod, a forked stick said to dip towards underground water.
explanation.definitionFit: To dowse is to search for water or minerals with a divining rod that points to where it lies.

clue.text: see 8dn.
Hot dish from Murdoch and Sun, beset by the awful wife?

indicators.note: awful means badly made, so the letters are jumbled
beset by others means surrounded by them

blocks.note: Iris Murdoch, the novelist, not Rupert
taken as written, then rearranged
S is the abbreviation for sun
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: Rupert Murdoch and his Sun newspaper plagued by a dreadful wife, a hot media story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Murdoch and Sun' points to Rupert and his tabloid, but Murdoch is the novelist Iris.
explanation.definitionFit: This stew of mutton, potatoes and onions is a traditional meal served warm from the pot.

clue.text: (& 15ac.) Harebrained as Cook's far from 100% effort?

blocks.note: first meaning: ill-conceived, foolish
second meaning: a cook's dish only partly done in the oven

explanation.surface: A foolish scheme by someone named Cook, who did not give it full effort.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital on 'Cook' suggests a person; it is just a cook whose bread is underdone.
explanation.definitionFit: A poorly thought-out plan is called this, as is food taken out of the oven before it is fully done.

clue.text: Independent infiltrating party, one pissed with 'the ultimate in Tory burden'

indicators.note: something infiltrating a group gets inside it
the ultimate letter of a word is its last

blocks.note: Lab is short for the Labour Party
I is the abbreviation for Independent
the Roman numeral for one
lit is slang for drunk
the last letter of Tory

explanation.surface: An independent joining a party alongside a drunk is the ultimate Tory headache.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' could be Tory given the surface, but the party here is Labour, abbreviated; 'lit' is slang for drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: A liability is something that holds you back or a debt you owe, a load that weighs on you.

clue.text: What LibDem candidates often do: accepting nothing is immoral

indicators.note: a word accepting another takes it in

blocks.note: Liberal Democrat candidates frequently fail to win their seats
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: A joke about Liberal Democrats habitually losing elections, and accepting nothing being wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The Liberal Democrats are a British third party that rarely wins seats.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose morals are lax ones, so a loose person is someone of dissolute, promiscuous conduct.
